sections.title: Adding information
sections.content:
Words that add ideas or information:
• furthermore — in addition (formal). The plan is expensive; furthermore, it's unlikely to work.
• moreover — what's more (formal). The hotel was dirty. Moreover, the staff were unhelpful.
• in addition to — as well as. In addition to English, she speaks French and Arabic.
• not only... but also — She is not only intelligent but also extremely hard-working.
• on top of that — (informal) additionally. The train was late. On top of that, it started raining.

sections.title: Contrasting and conceding
sections.content:
Words that show contrast or concession:
• although / even though — despite the fact. Although it rained, we enjoyed the trip.
• despite / in spite of — notwithstanding. Despite the risks, they went ahead with the plan.
• admittedly — acknowledging a point. Admittedly, the project is over budget.
• be that as it may — accepting a point but continuing. Be that as it may, we still need to find a solution.
• having said that — acknowledging but pivoting. The food was expensive. Having said that, the quality was excellent.

exercises.question: 'Furthermore' is used to:
exercises.hint: Adding more to what was said.
exercises.explanation: Furthermore is used to add extra information that supports the point.

exercises.question: 'Despite' is followed by:
exercises.explanation: Despite is followed by a noun or -ing form, not a clause.

exercises.question: 'Admittedly' is used when you:
exercises.explanation: Admittedly is used to acknowledge that something is true, often before countering it.

exercises.question: Which is the INFORMAL alternative to 'moreover'?
exercises.explanation: On top of that is the informal equivalent of 'moreover' or 'furthermore'.

exercises.question: 'Be that as it may' means:
exercises.hint: Accepting a point and moving on.
exercises.explanation: Be that as it may means accepting something while indicating it doesn't change the main argument.

exercises.question: 'Even though' is stronger than:
exercises.hint: Both show concession, one is more emphatic.
exercises.explanation: Even though is more emphatic than 'although', stressing the surprise of the contrast.

exercises.question: 'Having said that' is used to:
exercises.explanation: Having said that introduces a contrasting or qualifying statement.

exercises.question: 'Not only... but also' is used to:
exercises.hint: Two things are both true and noteworthy.
exercises.explanation: Not only... but also emphasises that two things are both true.
